newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Feb 26.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Feb 26.

text.p: - Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- TUC PLEDGE TO LIMIT STRIKES

The Trades Union Congress is expected to support proposals in a document entitled Partners for Progress which pledges to minimise industrial disputes and create a partnership with industry. In an interview with the Financial Times, the TUC general secretary John Monks spoke of creating "an active agenda with employers to improve corporate performance through improved training and increased investment".
-- LAW URGED ON COMPUTER DATE CHANGE 'BOMB'

The government is to come under increased pressure to legislate to ensure that computer companies take action to avert the millennium bomb' affecting older computers which will not be able to distinguish between 1900 and 2000. Several major companies are backing a private millennium computer compliance bill proposed by David Atkinson MP.
-- DISCOUNT HOUSE UNION TO CLOSE TRADING OPERATION

The discount house Union, once the most powerful in the UK, is to run down its trading books and begin redundancy talks with employees. This follows the Bank of England's decision to end its 200-year-old relationship with discount brokers next month when the Bank will start to use the new gilt sales and repurchases, or repo, market. Union's main rivals, Gerrard & King and Cater Allen, have become players in the repo market and will continue dealing with the Bank of England.
-- TORIES UNVEIL PLAN FOR SELLING LONDON TUBE

Transport Secretary George Young has confirmed that the government is to privatise London Underground, the capital's tube network which has been under public sector control for over 60 years. Young said on Tuesday that three options were being considered for the sale, which would be accompanied by a government commitment to plough back the bulk of the money raised into the network to clear a 1.2 billion sterling investment shortfall. News of the sale prompted immediate criticism from the opposition Labour party that the network was being sold at a fraction of its real value.
-- CREDIT LYONNAIS AID MAY BE TIED TO DISPOSALS

Troubled French state-controlled bank Credit Lyonnais is likely to be told by the European Commission to sell all its remaining European banking operations outside France before approval is given for a state-funded rescue package worth up to FFr30 billion (3.2 billion sterling). The controversial aid package, which comes on top of some FFr49 billion already given by the French government, is also likely to provoke demands for reductions in the bank's domestic branch network and the sale of parts of its wholesale banking interests.
-- ARMS EXPORT CASE RULES OUT DAMAGES FOR COMPANIES

A test case in the High Court has resulted in a ruling that companies which suffer financial loss because they are victims of miscarriages of justice cannot be awarded damages from government compensation schemes. The case was brought by arms exporting company Atlantic Commercial, which was claiming 500,000 sterling compensation after being wrongly convicted in 1985 of selling machines guns to Iraq.
-- PARTIES URGED TO ADOPT I.T. MANIFESTO

Britain's next government is being urged to adopt a 10-point manifesto aimed at preventing the country 'falling disastrously behind its competitors in the use and exploitation of information technology'. The manifesto has been drafted by the CCSA, the UK association for the software, IT services and information industries, and by software company Oracle. The plan, published on Tuesday and circulated to the main political parties, follows research which shows that the UK is falling behind the rest of the world in IT.
-- KVAERNER CUTS COSTS AS PROFITS FALL 70 PER CENT

Norwegian shipbuilding, engineering and construction group Kvaerner, which last year acquired the UK conglomerate Trafalgar House, has reported a 70 per cent fall in 1996 profits, from NKr2.4bn (221 million sterling) to NKr750 million. The fall, described by the group as 'most unsatisfactory', comes as Kvaerner grapples with its UK acquisition as well as seeing weak performances in several of its older businesses. A cost-cutting and restructuring operation at ailing units will continue.
-- EARLIER FATE FOR YORKSHIRE ELECTRICITY

The Office of Fair Trading has said that a decision on the 1.5 billion sterling agreed takeover bid for Yorkshire Electricity by two US utilities could be made by March 24. The announcement will raise hopes that the fate of the deal will be secured by the government before the forthcoming general election. The two US companies, American Electric Power and Public Service Company, have lodged a 'pre-notified' bid with the OFT, and analysts say they do not expect another bidder to enter the contest.
-- SHIRE IN 104 MILLION STERLING US PURCHASE

Fledgling UK drugs company Shire Pharmaceuticals has announced it is to acquire US drugs delivery company Pharmavene for up to 104.5 million sterling. The final amount to be paid depends on the performance of Pharmavene's lead product and on royalties received on all Pharmavene's products. Shire, which currently has 11 products in development, also announced plans to raise 11.5 million sterling from a placing and open offer of six million shares. The funds raised will go towards further acquisitions, including a European marketing company for about 10 million sterling.
